Detailed entries for `QPKG-033..QPKG-039`. Each follows the four-part
**What / Why / How / When NOT to apply** shape. "QDK guide" means
`docs/QDK-Developer-Guide.md` in [qnap-dev/QDK](https://github.com/qnap-dev/QDK).

---

## QPKG-033 — Never depend on `autorun.sh` or silently edit system init or cron

**What.** A package starts through its service script and the QPKG
lifecycle only. It does not install or depend on `autorun.sh`, and it does
not change system init scripts or cron entries other than its own clearly
marked lines (QPKG-032).

**Why.** Since QTS 4.3.3, `autorun.sh` runs only when the user enables
"Run user defined startup processes (autorun.sh)" in Control Panel
([QNAP FAQ](https://www.qnap.com/en/how-to/faq/article/running-your-own-application-at-startup),
2023-07-06), so a package that relies on it does not start for most users.
The QSnatch malware persisted on QNAP devices by modifying cron and init
scripts ([CISA AA20-209A](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa20-209a),
2020), so a package that edits that state without saying so looks exactly
like an infection to users and reviewers.

**How.** Put boot-time work in the service script's `start` (QPKG-015) and
declare ordering with `Dependency=` (QPKG-018).

**When NOT to apply.** Never for a distributed package. A personal script on
your own NAS is outside this skill.

## QPKG-034 — Plan for signature enforcement

**What.** Expect unsigned packages to be blocked. Document for users the
App Center setting "Allow installation and execution of applications without
a digital signature". Treat `QNAP_CODE_SIGNING=1` as available only to
packages built in QNAP's own pipeline; a third party gets a QNAP-signed
package only through the App Center submission process.

**Why.** The setting is off by default on QTS 5.0 and later, and even with it
on, App Center refuses packages whose signature was tampered with
([QTS 5.0 App Center settings](https://docs.qnap.com/operating-system/qts/5.0.x/en-us/app-center-settings-8C55F8A1.html)).
Signatures are also checked at runtime: users on QTS 5.2.7 saw "has an
invalid digital signature. The app has stopped"
([QNAP community, 2025-10-05](https://community.qnap.com/t/2500)).
`QNAP_CODE_SIGNING=1` signs against QNAP's code-signing server and verifies at
install; the QDK template notes it "currently can be done only inside QNAP"
(QDK guide §14).

**How.**

```sh
# qpkg.cfg for a third-party package: leave QNAP code signing off
# QNAP_CODE_SIGNING="1"
```

State in the install docs that the unsigned-app setting is required, and that
a firmware update may turn it off again.

**When NOT to apply.** Packages distributed through the official App Center
are signed by QNAP during publication.

## QPKG-035 — Never repack a vendor-signed QPKG; patch at runtime instead

**What.** To change a QNAP-signed package such as QuObjects, do not unpack,
edit and rebuild it. Install it unmodified, and apply the change from a
separate package (or script) at each `start`: back up the original file once,
patch it, verify the patch landed, log when it did not, and restore the
original on `stop`. Gate the patch on the vendor package's version.

**Why.** Rebuilding invalidates QNAP's signature, and App Center refuses a
tampered signature even when unsigned apps are allowed (QPKG-034). Vendor
packages also update automatically ("Install all required updates
automatically"), which overwrites any patch, so a one-time edit silently
reverts. OneCD's
[HideThatBanner](https://github.com/OneCDOnly/HideThatBanner) is a working
example of the runtime pattern.

**How.**

```sh
target=$(/sbin/getcfg OSS Install_Path -f /etc/config/qpkg.conf)/oss/conf/example.conf
ver=$(/sbin/getcfg OSS Version -f /etc/config/qpkg.conf)
case "$ver" in 2.5.1289) ;; *) /sbin/log_tool -t1 -uSystem -p127.0.0.1 -mlocalhost -a "patch: untested OSS $ver, skipped"; exit 0 ;; esac
[ -f "$target.orig" ] || cp -p "$target" "$target.orig"
sed 's/^old_value$/new_value/' "$target.orig" > "$target"
cmp -s "$target" "$target.orig" && /sbin/log_tool -t2 -uSystem -p127.0.0.1 -mlocalhost -a "patch: did not apply"
```

**When NOT to apply.** When the change is large, replacing the vendor app with
an open-source one you package yourself is simpler and avoids QPKG-039.

## QPKG-036 — Unpack untrusted packages with `head`/`tail` and `tar`

**What.** To inspect a `.qpkg` you did not build, read the offsets from its
header (`script_len`, the `expr $script_len + N` line, the `f.seek(N)` data
length), cut the sections out with `head -c` / `tail -c`, and list each
tarball before extracting it, as an unprivileged user in an empty directory.
Never run the file, and never use `qbuild --extract` on it.

**Why.** A `.qpkg` is a shell script followed by its payloads, so running it
runs the vendor's installer. `qbuild --extract` is not safe either: its
`extract_qpkg` pulls shell lines out of the package header with `sed` and
`eval`s them, which runs code from the package.

**How.**

```sh
q=app.qpkg
S=$(grep -a -m1 -oE '^script_len=[0-9]+' "$q" | cut -d= -f2)
C=$(grep -a -m1 -oE 'expr \$script_len \+ [0-9]+' "$q" | grep -oE '[0-9]+$')
N=$(grep -a -m1 -oE 'f\.seek\([0-9]+\)' "$q" | grep -oE '[0-9]+')
tail -c +$((S + 1)) "$q" | head -c "$C" | tar -xO > control.tar.gz
tail -c +$((S + C + 1)) "$q" | head -c "$N" > data.tar.gz
tar -tzf data.tar.gz | grep -E '^/|(^|/)\.\.(/|$)' && echo "unsafe paths"
mkdir data && tar -xzf data.tar.gz -C data --no-same-owner
```

The remaining bytes after the data archive are the signature area and the
QDK tail.

**When NOT to apply.** Packages you built yourself in CI can use
`qbuild --query` and `--extract` (QPKG-006).

## QPKG-037 — Never ship default credentials

**What.** A package that needs credentials (an admin password, S3 access and
secret keys) generates them at install time, stores them in a file with mode
`0600` inside the package or data dir, and passes them to the service by file
rather than on the command line.

**Why.** Many upstreams ship well-known defaults (RustFS:
`rustfsadmin`/`rustfsadmin`). A NAS is often reachable from the LAN or
through myQNAPcloud, so default credentials are an open door. Credentials on
the command line are visible to every user in `ps`.

**How.**

```sh
pkg_install() {
    mkdir -p "$SYS_QPKG_DIR/etc"
    umask 077
    [ -f "$SYS_QPKG_DIR/etc/secret_key" ] ||
        head -c 32 /dev/urandom | od -An -tx1 | tr -d ' \n' > "$SYS_QPKG_DIR/etc/secret_key"
}
# service script
export APP_SECRET_KEY_FILE="$QPKG_ROOT/etc/secret_key"
```

**When NOT to apply.** Never for a network service.

## QPKG-038 — Give package dirs least-privilege modes

**What.** Files and directories the package installs are owned by root (or
the service user) with modes no wider than they need: `0755` for
directories and binaries, `0644` for config, `0600` for secrets. Never
`chmod 777` a package directory to let another process write to it.

**Why.** The package runs as root (QPKG-012), and files in its directory are
read or executed by that root service. A world-writable directory lets any
local user or compromised process replace a config or script the root
service then loads. QNAP's own QuObjects runs `chmod 777` on its Swift config
directory so the web-server user can write one file.

**How.** Grant only the file that needs it:

```sh
touch "$SYS_QPKG_DIR/swift/etc/swift/cors.json"
chown httpdusr "$SYS_QPKG_DIR/swift/etc/swift/cors.json"
chmod 0644 "$SYS_QPKG_DIR/swift/etc/swift/cors.json"
```

**When NOT to apply.** Never.

## QPKG-039 — Do not redistribute modified QNAP packages or decompiled code

**What.** Keep a patched or unpacked QNAP package, and any decompiled QNAP
code, on your own systems. Share the patch method (QPKG-035), not the
modified package or code.

**Why.** QNAP's Software Terms of Use §4 prohibit distributing the licensed
software, modifying it, creating derivative works and decompiling it
([QNAP Software Terms of Use](https://www.qnap.com/en/legal/qnap-software-terms-of-use),
revised 2026-10-01). Open-source components bundled inside keep their own
licenses (§5), but QNAP's glue code does not.

**How.** Publish the runtime patch script, which downloads nothing from QNAP
and edits the user's own installed copy, or replace the vendor app with an
open-source one.

**When NOT to apply.** Open-source components inside the package (for
example OpenStack Swift in QuObjects) can be used under their own licenses,
taken from their upstream source rather than from the QNAP package.
